newsitem.title: USA: Sallie Mae CEO aims to break deadlock by resigning.
newsitem.headline: Sallie Mae CEO aims to break deadlock by resigning.

text.p: Sallie Mae Chief Executive Lawrence Hough said Wednesday he will resign in a move aimed at breaking a deadlock and ending a months-long battle for control of the government-backed lending company.
The Student Loan Marketing Association, or Sallie Mae, said Hough will remain with the company through a transition to a private company and until a successor is named.
The news sparked a jump in Sallie Mae shares, which were up $4 to $124.25 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Sallie Mae is a stockholder-owned, government-sponsored company that is the nation's largest source of funding for post-secondary education loans.

It has been engulfed in a struggle between its management, dominated by banking executives, and an opposition shareholder group. The opposition group, the Committee to Restore Value, wants Sallie Mae to originate loans directly rather than just buying student loans from banks and other lenders and securitizing the loans.

"I intend to break the deadlock and free the new CEO to pursue continued growth in franchise and share value," Hough said. "We should not permit continued turmoil to undermine Sallie Mae's strength in the marketplace and support on Capitol Hill."
Sallie Mae said David Vitale, a vice chairman of First Chicago NBD Corp. and a Sallie Mae director for 20 years, was being proposed to become non-executive chairman.
In an interview, Vitale said the firm had missed out on $250 million of business "in the current quarter" as a result of the argument between Sallie Mae management and the CRV.
However, he noted that the deterioration was in comparison with a "couple billion" of dollars in business it did in the quarter, and said it would not have a material impact on the quarter's results.
Sallie Mae and the Committee to Restore Value have been dueling since January, with both sides supporting the idea of ending Sallie Mae's government ties but each disagreeing on business strategy.

Sallie Mae has argued that if it begins originating loans, it will be perceived as a competitor to the banks that bring it a lot of business. "Lenders are simply saying 'We don't want to work with a competitor,'" Vitale said in an interview.
"In the event of a change in control, then you'll see cannibalization of our business in a dramatic way," he added.

A shareholder vote on privatisation and competing slates of directors is expected in July after neither the management nor the Committee to Restore Value was able to garner a majority for its proposals at meetings held in May.

Hough, who has been chief executive since 1990, said that to resolve the situation, it will be necessary to turn to a chief executive "who draws from a non-government-sponsored enterprise background and experience."
The Committee to Restore Value is headed by Albert Lord, who was chief operating officer when he left Sallie Mae in 1994.
The committee succeeded in getting eight people elected to the Sallie Mae board in 1995.
